question.headline: Keep the cost-saving offer, or build the revenue one?
question.asked: My business mentor told me it is easier to sell something that makes people money than something that saves them cost. I currently sell email agents that save cost - that offer is fully worked out and I can sell it easily today. The alternative is helping sales managers and their teams quote faster and respond to customers faster, which would make them money - but I have not worked that out at all yet. This is my business (Glimps, AI chatbots and agents for small and mid-sized companies in Belgium) and it decides where my revenue comes from. What do I do?

verdict.read: Your mentor is right about positioning, not about product. The email agent already saves cost and speeds up replies - that is a revenue story you haven't told yet.

quotes.text: not stop doing that. Like if it keeps working, you keep doing it.
when you have a starving crowd when the supply demand curve is in your favor it's hard to not make money

call.heading: Keep the offer, change the story
call.text: Don't build a second product. Sell the same email agent to sales teams, led by speed to quote and faster replies. If ten conversations prove that story lands harder, then build.

actions.do: Rewrite your pitch around revenue, not cost saved
actions.how: Same product, new headline: quotes out faster, replies same day
actions.detail:
Your email agent already does the work a revenue pitch needs. It reads the inbox, drafts the reply, and gets a quote out while the buyer is still warm. You have simply been selling the hour it saves instead of the deal it wins.

Hormozi's move: the offer is the same, the promise changes. Stop saying it saves your team six hours a week. Say every enquiry gets an answer the same day, and quotes go out in minutes instead of days.

Keenan's move: put a number on the gap. Ask how many enquiries went cold last month because nobody replied in time. That number is your price.

actions.do: Test the revenue story in ten real conversations
actions.how: Pitch it to sales managers this month, build nothing yet
actions.detail:
Ten conversations is enough to settle this, and it costs you nothing but time. Book them with sales managers, not owners - the manager feels the slow quote every day.

Rackham's move: ask what a late quote costs them. How often does a prospect go quiet while they wait? What happens to the deal when a competitor answers first? Let them do the arithmetic out loud.

Then count. If the revenue story pulls harder than your cost pitch, you have found the hungrier crowd and you already own the product. If it doesn't, your mentor's rule does not hold in your market, and you go back to selling what works.

dissent.text: Blount pushed back hard: a new story means nothing if nobody hears it. The bottleneck may be your outreach volume, not your positioning.
dissent.full:
Blount's objection is the one worth keeping. He does not argue that the revenue framing is wrong - he argues it is not the constraint. If you are only having four sales conversations a month, a better story gets you a better four, and four is still four.

His position: fix the volume first. Same offer, same pitch, twenty conversations instead of four, and the market tells you the answer far faster than a repositioning exercise does.

The bench sided with Hormozi because you cannot know which story to scale until you have tested both. But Blount is right that the test is worthless if you only run it three times.

verdict.vote_label: The vote — each adviser names who should make the call

pn.label: What next
pn.sub: Copy a line into the chat

speeches.name: Alex Hormozi
speeches.text: Your mentor gave you a rule about positioning and you heard it as a rule about product. Those are not the same thing. The email agent you already sell answers enquiries faster - that is revenue. Don't build a second thing so you can say a sentence you could say today.

quote.text: not stop doing that. Like if it keeps working, you keep doing it.

speeches.name: Dale Carnegie
speeches.text: Carnegie's principle: talk in terms of the other person's interest. A sales manager does not lie awake about overhead. He lies awake about the enquiry that went cold on Friday. Say it his way and it is the same product.

speeches.name: Jim Keenan
speeches.text: Gap selling says the offer is whatever closes the gap between where they are and where they want to be. Cost saved and money made are two descriptions of one gap. Go find out which side of it your buyer actually feels.

speeches.name: Neil Rackham
speeches.text: This is what implication questions are for. A slow quote is a small cost until you ask what it costs - then it becomes lost deals. You do not need a new product to move a problem from minor to serious.

speeches.name: David Sandler
speeches.text: Before you build anything for sales managers, qualify them. Do they have budget, do they decide, and do they hurt enough to move? A market you have never sold into is not a plan, it is a hope.

speeches.name: Chris Voss
speeches.text: Let their language pick the framing. Ask a sales manager what happens when a quote takes three days, then listen for the words he uses. Those words are your pitch, and you did not have to invent them.

speeches.name: Jeb Blount
speeches.text: I'll be the difficult one. Positioning is not your constraint, activity is. A perfect story told to four people a month loses to a decent story told to thirty. Fix the number of conversations before you rewrite the script.

speeches.name: Jordan Belfort
speeches.text: You will sell whichever one you actually believe. Right now you believe in the email agent because you have done the work. Chasing a story you have not built yet will show up in your voice on the first call.

conclusion.label: Where round one landed
conclusion.text: Seven seats say the same thing: the revenue story is a reframe of what you already own, not a new product. Blount wants the volume question answered first.

speeches.name: Jeb Blount
speeches.text: Alex, you are solving the wrong bottleneck. He has one finished offer and he is asking whether to build a second. Neither answer helps if he is only in four conversations a month. Volume is the test, not the wording.

speeches.name: Alex Hormozi
speeches.text: Volume without a story just spreads a weak message faster. But you are right that the test needs numbers. Run the reframe at higher volume - that is one experiment, not two.

speeches.name: David Sandler
speeches.text: Then be honest about what the test proves. Ten conversations with sales managers who cannot buy proves nothing. Qualify the seat first, or you will read a no as a verdict on your story.

speeches.name: Jim Keenan
speeches.text: Volume hides the diagnosis, Jeb. Thirty conversations with the wrong framing gets thirty polite refusals and no idea why. He needs the gap named before he scales anything.

conclusion.label: Where round two left it
conclusion.text: The bench agrees on the move and splits on the sequence. Hormozi and Keenan want the story fixed first; Blount wants the numbers up first. Sandler wants the buyer qualified before either.

ballot.why: It's an offer question before a volume one
Talk in terms of the other's interest
The gap is revenue, not hours saved
Implication questions turn cost into revenue
Qualify the new market before building it
Nothing sells if the pipeline stays empty
Their words decide the framing, not ours
Conviction needs a story worth believing

ballot_note: The chair never votes for himself.
